'''''Menispermum canadense''''', the '''Canadian moonseed''', '''common moonseed''', or '''yellow parilla''', is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Menispermaceae]], native to eastern North America, from southern Canada south to northern Florida, and from the Atlantic coast west to Manitoba and Texas.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=220008359 |work=[[Flora of North America]] |title=''Menispermum canadense'' }}</ref> It occurs in thickets, moist woods, and the banks of streams.

==Description==

It is a woody climbing [[vine]] growing to {{Convert|6|m|abbr=off}} tall. The [[leaves]] are palmately lobed, {{Convert|5–20|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} in diameter with 3–7 shallow lobes, occasionally rounded and unlobed. The fruit are produced in {{cvt|6–10|cm|frac=4}} diameter clusters of purple-black [[Berry (botany)|berries]], each berry is {{cvt|1–1.5|cm|frac=3}} in diameter. The seed inside the berry resembles a [[Lunar phase|crescent moon]], and is responsible for the common name. The fruit is ripe between September and October, the same general time frame in which wild grapes are ripe. Both the leaves and fruit resemble those of grapes; confusion can be dangerous as moonseed fruit is [[poison]]ous.

The root is a [[rhizome]], so one specimen can form colonies of genetically identical plants.

== Toxicity ==
All parts of these plants are known to be poisonous.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20121017131304/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/plantox/textResults.cfm?q=Menispermum+canadense FDA Poisonous Plant Database]</ref> The principal toxin is the [[alkaloid]] [[dauricine]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/poison/Menisca.htm |title=''Menispermum canadense'' |work=Poisonous Plants of North Carolina, Alice B. Russell Department of Horticultural Science; James W. Hardin, Larry Grand, and Angela Fraser |publisher=North Carolina State University |access-date=9 April 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090116030040/http://www.ces.ncsu.edu/depts/hort/consumer/poison/Menisca.htm |archive-date=16 January 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The fruit of Canadian moonseed are poisonous and can be fatal. While foraging for [[Wild grape|wild grapes]], one should examine the seeds of the fruit to make sure one is not eating moonseeds: moonseeds have a single [[crescent]]-shaped seed, while grapes have round seeds. Differences in taste should also be an indicator of whether or not a specimen is grape or moonseed, moonseeds have a taste that is described as "rank"{{Citation needed|date=November 2025}}. Also, the moonseed vine lacks [[tendril]]s, whilst the vine of the wild grape has forked [[tendril]]s.<ref>Peterson, Lee, "A Field Guide to Edible Wild Plants of Eastern and Central North America", p. 50, Houghton Mifflin Company, New York City, accessed 22 November 2010. {{ISBN|0-395-20445-3 }}</ref>

== Uses ==
The [[Cherokee]] used moonseed as a [[laxative]], and as a [[gynecological]] and [[venereal]] aid. The root was used for skin diseases. The [[Lenape]] used it in a [[salve]] for sores on the skin.<ref>[http://naeb.brit.org/uses/species/2439/ Native American Ethnobotany Database (University of Michigan – Dearborn): Moonseed]</ref> It has been used for a variety of medicinal uses by [[Americas|Americans]] of European descent.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/duke/ethnobot.pl?ethnobot.taxon=Menispermum%20canadense |title=Dr. Duke's Database of USDA GRIN Taxonomy: Canadian Moonseed |access-date=7 March 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923174025/http://www.ars-grin.gov/cgi-bin/duke/ethnobot.pl?ethnobot.taxon=Menispermum%20canadense |archive-date=23 September 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
